strandingSteps: Keep your distance and keep people and dogs away.
Don’t push it back into the sea.
Note the location and take photos if it’s safe.
Call your local stranding network straight away.
reports.ctaText: A few details and a photo are all it takes. Your report helps researchers follow these animals through the seasons.

stranding.title: Found a stranded
stranding.intro: Stay calm, keep your distance and call for help. Trained responders know what to do — a quick call is the most useful thing you can do.
stranding.callText: If the animal is alive, or you’re not sure who to contact, call the European emergency number. They’ll alert the local authorities and the stranding network.
do: Keep a safe distance, and keep people and dogs away.
Note the exact location, the time, and the animal’s size and condition.
Take photos from a distance, if it’s safe to do so.
Stay nearby until help arrives, if you can.
dont: Don’t push or drag it back into the sea — it’s probably sick or exhausted and will often strand again.
Don’t touch it: marine mammals can pass diseases to people and pets.
Don’t pull on its flippers or tail, or cover its blowhole.
Don’t take bones, teeth or other parts — these are protected species.
stranding.deadText: Report it anyway. Dead animals tell scientists a great deal about the health, diet and threats facing the population.
stranding.networksIntro: Trained teams who respond to strandings and study the animals they find.
stranding.noNetworks: Call {number} or the Polícia Marítima — they will alert the regional team.
stranding.ctaText: Add a report on WhaleTale too, so the record isn’t lost.

report.title: Share what
report.intro: Every record — a passing dolphin, a whale on the horizon, a seal on the beach — helps researchers understand which animals use our waters, where and when.
report.notice: The online report form is coming soon. In the meantime, keep your notes and photos: every record counts.
report.sightingTitle: A sighting at sea or from shore
report.sightingText: What to note, so your record is as useful as possible:
sightingChecklist: Where you were — GPS coordinates if possible
Species, if you know it, and how many animals
What they were doing: feeding, travelling, resting…
Photos, especially of the dorsal fin and tail
report.sightingLink: Not sure what you saw? Browse species
report.strandingText: If an animal is stranded right now, don’t wait for a form. Call for help first.

about.title: A field guide
about.intro: WhaleTale brings together the science of the whales, dolphins, porpoises and seals of Portuguese waters — from the mainland coast to the Azores and Madeira — and invites everyone to help study them.

mission.title: Learn
mission.text: Peer-reviewed science in plain language, in Portuguese, English and French.

mission.title: Observe
mission.text: Species profiles and field tips to help you recognise what you see, and where and when to look.

mission.title: Contribute
mission.text: Sightings and stranding reports that add to what we know about these animals.

about.methodologyIntro: Trust is everything for a science resource. These are the rules we hold ourselves to.
methodology: Facts come from peer-reviewed research and standard references, such as the IUCN Red List and the Portuguese Red Book of Mammals.
Where studies disagree, we give ranges or rounded values rather than a single, falsely precise figure.
Every page lists the sources behind it.
Field reports are checked before they join the record.
Spotted a mistake? Tell us and we’ll correct it.
about.partnersIntro: WhaleTale is independent. Partners help us grow, but never decide what we say.
policy: Partners and sponsors have no say over scientific content.
Sponsored features are always clearly labelled.
No sponsorship ever appears in the stranding or reporting pages, or inside the science content.
We don’t accept support from organisations whose activities conflict with the protection of marine mammals.
about.partnersEmpty: We’re looking for our first partners: research groups, NGOs and foundations that share our mission.
about.contactText: Spotted an error, know a resource we missed, or want to work with us? We’d love to hear from you.
